### 读码

条码用于跟踪与识别整个供应链中的原材料和制成品。条码包括一维条码和二维码，例如零售产品上的 UPC 码和包装上的 DataMatrix 码。

[读码器](/zh-cn/products/barcode-readers-and-scanners)可以高速处理信息，并正确读取部分撕裂、模糊、脏污或变形的条码。图像扫码器收集读取的条码图像，对未读或误读的情况进行分析并找出原因，例如打印头堵塞、条码损坏或光线不足。在所有条码并未按照相同方式定向时，多个相机系统可以同时从部件或包装的多个侧面进行扫描，以提高读码速率。

**示例：**

![DataMan 80 barcode reader scans code on label](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcog-p-001.sitecorecontenthub.cloud%2Fapi%2Fpublic%2Fcontent%2Fa68d72ae958d4442bd9966c61d9d1219%3Fv%3Ddf0a0610%26t%3D16x9w936h526&w=2048&q=75)

![自动化代码读取和光学字符识别基本指南](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcog-p-001.sitecorecontenthub.cloud%2Fapi%2Fpublic%2Fcontent%2F94c0a535d8114a4098b486ad4577c0df%3Fv%3D297227d7%26t%3D16x9w373h210&w=2048&q=75)

## 代码读取和 OCR 自动化必备指南

### 阅读文本：OCR 和 OCV

条码在现代工业中无处不在，但人类可读的印刷文本仍必不可少，特别是在零售、制造、[医药](/zh-cn/industries/pharmaceutical-and-medical-device-solutions)及[食品和饮料](/zh-cn/industries/fast-moving-consumer-goods/food-and-beverage)供应链中，以标识保质期、[批号](/zh-cn/applications/optical-character-recognition/date-and-lot-code-inspection)及其他重要信息。为使该文本内容可用于现代高速处理流程，必须让其可被机器准确读取。机器视觉系统可以用毫秒级速度、以 99.99% 的准确度读取此类条码。

光学字符识别 (OCR) 和光学字符验证 (OCV) 均可以识别并解析图像中的文本，但两者存在一个关键区别。OCR 读取文本后会触发另一项操作，而 OCV 则按照已知标准验证文本质量。

**示例：**

检查保质期或批号是否印刷正确 (OCV)。

![Cognex vision systems perform OCR on cigarette tax stamps to verify text](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcog-p-001.sitecorecontenthub.cloud%2Fapi%2Fpublic%2Fcontent%2F990f473c0f6d43628fc4518092645daa%3Fv%3De249665b%26t%3D16x9w936h526&w=2048&q=75)

辨别鉴定假冒产品 (OCR)。

![In-Sight 3800 vision system reads barcode and characters directly marked on a metal pacemaker surface](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcog-p-001.sitecorecontenthub.cloud%2Fapi%2Fpublic%2Fcontent%2F02b49cf1c46d4d0a80ccb0da93d111ff%3Fv%3D3181ae02%26t%3D16x9w936h526&w=2048&q=75)

建立可追溯性，以满足监管要求 (OCR)。

This is a Cognex webpage (in Chinese) explaining the types of machine vision systems and their applications. The content covers the three main categories of machine vision systems:
1. **Line scan cameras** - Used for continuous inspection applications such as web manufacturing (fabrics, paper, soft goods), capturing wide, thin images that are reconstructed line-by-line as material moves through the scan area. Faster than standard 2D cameras for these applications.
2. **2D/Area scan systems** - The most common type of machine vision. These range from simple single-purpose sensors (lower cost, smaller, easier to deploy, more robust) to more comprehensive systems (more configurable, capable of more complex tasks, larger/higher-resolution images). Selection depends on task, data output format, cost, and ease of use.
3. **3D vision systems** - Add image depth, sometimes using lasers to measure distance and calculate depth. While adding complexity and cost, depth information is critical for applications like guiding robotic arms to precisely grasp objects regardless of position, and automating complex cutting and welding processes.

The webpage also details what machine vision can do, using the GIGI acronym (Guidance, Identification, Gauging, Inspection):
- **Defect detection**: Machine vision outperforms manual inspection by operating at high speed on production lines without fatigue, detecting even unexpected tiny defects, and storing information for continuous production improvement. Examples include finding loose connectors, poorly soldered wires, bad seams, defective photovoltaic cells, semiconductor wafer or EV battery defects, and contaminants in food products.
- **Object detection and counting**: Used for inventory management, production lines, and shipment release/acceptance. Examples include verifying electronic components on PCBs, detecting presence of components like clips, screws, springs, labels, seals, manuals or inserts, and counting products in packaging or on pallets.
- **Measurement and gauging**: Machine vision enables precise measurement (distance, area, diameter) at micron-level precision at high speed, with consistent and accurate results, storing images and related data for warranty or compliance issues. Examples include measuring dimensions of cast/injection-molded parts, circularity and angles of part tips, and label positions or package dimensions.
- **Finding, guiding, and locating parts**: Machine vision locates parts on conveyors or in bins, guides robots for pick-and-place and precise assembly with micron-level accuracy, and communicates position corrections to robots or PLCs. Examples include locating parts on conveyors for inspection, guiding robots on automotive assembly lines, and microchip assembly requiring micron-level precision.
- **Barcode reading**: Barcodes (1D and 2D codes like UPC and DataMatrix) track and identify raw materials and finished goods throughout the supply chain. Readers handle high-speed processing and can read torn, blurry, dirty, or deformed barcodes. Image-based scanners analyze unread/misread codes to diagnose causes. Multiple camera systems can scan from multiple sides simultaneously for better read rates. Examples include tracking packages in logistics warehouses, ensuring correct component assembly, and medical supply traceability.
- **OCR and OCV (text reading)**: Human-readable printed text remains essential (expiry dates, batch/lot numbers) in retail, manufacturing, pharmaceutical, and food/beverage supply chains. Machine vision reads such text at millisecond speeds with 99.99% accuracy. OCR triggers another action after reading text, while OCV verifies text quality against known standards. Examples include classifying parts by printed characters (OCR), verifying expiry dates/lot numbers (OCV), identifying counterfeit products (OCR), and establishing traceability for regulatory compliance (OCR).

The page concludes with promotional content on rule-based vs. AI-driven machine vision, an AI report, and a guide on EV manufacturing cost reduction, plus Cognex company information (headquarters: One Vision Drive, Natick, MA 01760-2059, USA).

URL: https://pdf.dfcfw.com/pdf/H3_AP202409201639950598_1.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a KPMG China industry insight report (September 2024) titled "智启未来：新质生产力引擎驱动下的智能制造行业革新" (Smart Future: Intelligent Manufacturing Industry Innovation Driven by New Quality Productive Forces), comprehensively reviewing the development of China's intelligent manufacturing (智能制造) sector.

**Key Sections and Findings:**

**1. Development History of Intelligent Manufacturing:**
- **Initial stage (1980s):** The concept was first introduced by American scholar Wright Bourne in his book "Smart Manufacturing." Japan developed the IMS (Intelligent Manufacturing System) concept emphasizing human-machine integration. Characterized by automation equipment and computer technology integration, CAD/CAE/CAPP/CAM tools, ERP/MRPII systems, and CIMS solutions.
- **Development stage (1990s):** Digitalization and networking deepened with Internet technology. "Internet+" manufacturing enabled connectivity between products, manufacturing, and services, shifting production from product-centric to user-centric models.
- **Maturity stage (21st century):** Big data, cloud computing, and AI applications. Major countries launched strategies including US "Advanced Manufacturing National Strategy" and "Industrial Internet," Germany's "Industry 4.0" with Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), Japan's AI and robotics strategies, EU's digital transformation plans, and China's "Made in China 2025." AI market projected to reach $184.04 billion in 2024 and exceed $800 billion by 2030 (Statista).

**2. China's Current Status:**
- **Policy evolution in four phases:** Starter period (2005-2014), Formation period (2015-2016, with "Made in China 2025"), Growth period (2017-2020, with "New Generation AI Development Plan"), and Deepening period (2021-present, with "14th Five-Year Smart Manufacturing Development Plan" establishing a "two-step" strategy: by 2025 most large industrial enterprises achieve digitalization/network adoption; by 2035 full digitalization with backbone enterprises basically intelligent).

--- SOURCE 11: 1工业之眼（Industrial Eye） ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06966

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic survey paper titled "Embodied Intelligence for Flexible Manufacturing: A Survey" (面向柔性制造的具身智能综述) published in April 2025 (volume 47, number 4, DOI: 250208). The paper is authored by XU Kai (National University of Defense Technology), ZHAO Hang (Wuhan University), HU Ruizhen (Shenzhen University), YANG Min and ZHANG Hui (Hunan University), and LIU Hao and YU Haibin (Shenyang Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences). Corresponding author is 徐凯 (kevin.kai.xu@gmail.com).

**Overview & Motivation:**
The survey addresses the rapid penetration of embodied intelligence (EI) into industrial manufacturing, driven by breakthroughs in modern AI (e.g., DeepSeek, GPT-4). Industrial scenarios—being semi-structured with stable operating conditions and standardized processes—are poised to become the first domain for large-scale adoption of EI. However, the shift toward "high product variety and small batch sizes" flexible manufacturing introduces new challenges: multi-type mixed-model production lines, rapid product iteration, and unstructured/non-standardized processes.

**Three Core Challenges in Flexible Manufacturing:**
1. **Accurate process modeling and monitoring under limited sensing** – production processes often can only observe partial environmental information due to viewing range, precision limits, and occlusion, making modeling difficult (e.g., single-view cameras cannot cover full large workpieces; bolts' internal physics cannot be observed).
2. **Dynamic balance between flexible adaptation and high-precision manipulation** – manufacturing must maintain precision (e.g., automotive assembly to ±0.05mm) while flexibly adapting to varied products; low-precision production lines must still achieve high-precision processes (e.g., new energy vehicle lines mixing multiple models).
3. **Coordinating general robotic skills with specialized industrial procedures** – systems need both cross-domain basic skills (grasping, placement, assembly, screwing, trajectory tracking) and expert-level process-specific skills (e.g., welding robots need both seam tracking and welding process knowledge).

**Survey Structure (Three Dimensions):**
1. **Industrial Eye (感知层/Perception):** Multimodal data fusion and real-time modeling in complex dynamic environments.
2. **Industrial Hand (控制层/Control):** Flexible, adaptive, precise manipulation for complex manufacturing processes.
3. **Industrial Brain (决策层/Decision):** Intelligent optimization methods for process planning and line scheduling.

**Key Technical Sections:**

*Section 1 – Industrial Eye:*
- **3D visual high-precision imaging:** Covers structured light (sub-millimeter precision, 0.1m–5m range), time-of-flight (centimeter precision, 0.1m–10m), and multi-view RGB imaging (centimeter precision, 0.5m–50m). Key methods include Fourier Transform Profilometry, Phase-Shifting Profilometry, Phase Measuring Deflectometry (PMD) for high-reflective surfaces, and neural methods (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting, DUSt3R, VGGT). Case studies include car paint surface reconstruction using PMD (reducing miss-rate to <1% and false-positive rate to <3%) and ship welding imaging using FoundationStereo achieving ±0.2mm depth reconstruction.
- **Multimodal data fusion:** Covers feature extraction for RGB, depth/point clouds, acoustics, and infrared modalities; heterogeneous feature alignment (CLIP, attention mechanisms, contrastive learning); and early/middle/late fusion strategies. Case studies include Stanford's multimodal assembly using VAE with Product of Experts (visual-tactile-proprioceptive fusion) and Shanghai Jiao Tong University's welding quality monitoring combining visual, acoustic, and electrical signals to predict defects 0-2 seconds in advance.
- **Industrial vision foundation models:** Discusses self-supervised pretraining (MIM, contrastive learning, teacher-student frameworks like DINO), 2D-to-3D foundation models (SAM/SAM 2, Depth Anything, FoundationPose, DINOv2, DUSt3R, VGGT), and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, Adapter Tuning, Prompt Tuning). Case studies include AnomalyDINO for few-shot defect detection and DUSt3R for low-texture image matching.

*Section 2 – Industrial Hand:*
- **Precise control with low-precision hardware:** Covers pose recognition (2D RGB-based and 3D point-cloud-based methods like MIRETR), control strategies (traditional PID/LQR/fuzzy vs. imitation learning vs. reinforcement learning vs. hybrid IL+RL), and Sim2Real transfer (domain randomization, Real2Sim2Real pipelines using Gaussian Splatting). Case studies include Tsinghua's digital twin + residual policy for 3C product assembly and Stanford's ALOHA system achieving millimeter-level precision on hardware under $20,000 (improving success rate from 60% to 96% and reducing operation cycles by 30-40%).
- **Flexible operations on variable production lines:** Covers general control strategy learning (policy distillation, meta-learning), interaction representation design (affordance, 2D and 3D representations), and decision foundation models ("plan-then-execute" LLM-based approaches like Palm-E, SayCan, Embodied-GPT, and end-to-end VLA models like OpenVLA, π0.5, 3D-VLA). Case studies include NVIDIA's policy distillation achieving >80% success across 80 assembly tasks and RoboGrind's LLM-guided grinding control (aviation blade shape deviation within ±0.03mm, wind turbine blade roughness Ra≤0.8μm).
- **Adaptive process parameter regulation:** Covers welding (CNN/MLP adaptive control, RL-based molten pool width control), grinding (data-driven parameter matching, IPSO-GRNN models, meta-RL approaches), and assembly (RL-based fastening, visual servo control). Case studies include University of Kentucky's data-driven arc welding control converging molten pool width in just 7 control cycles, and Huazhong University's MAML-PPO-based grinding parameter adaptation.

*Section 3 – Industrial Brain:*
- **Factory intelligent scheduling:** Covers Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP, NP-hard), learning-based scheduling (graph neural networks, multi-agent RL like the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics smart workshop system), autonomous mobile unit path planning (TSP/VRP, RL and diffusion-based solvers like DIFUSCO, DISCO), and material warehousing optimization (online bin packing via deep RL; CDRL, PCT methods). Case studies include an industrial online packing system achieving 57.4% space utilization (~19 boxes per pallet, ~10 seconds per box).
- **Digital twin virtual-real synchronization:** Discusses virtual model creation, state-aware synchronization, and twin-based intelligent scheduling (ISO definition: "digital mapping of observable manufacturing elements synchronized with actual manufacturing elements").

**Future Directions:**
The paper proposes a three-stage evolution model for embodied intelligence in flexible manufacturing: **cognition enhancement → skill transition → system evolution** (认知增强-技能跃迁-系统进化). It also discusses humanoid robots combining eye-hand-brain capabilities for factory environments and outlines future challenges, emphasizing multi-level technical collaboration and interdisciplinary integration (robotics, machine vision, AI) for closing the perception-decision-action loop.

**Focus Scope:** The survey focuses on discrete manufacturing (assembly, machining, inspection through explicit process sequences), explicitly excluding process manufacturing (continuous material and recipe processing).

**Funding:** Supported by multiple Chinese national and provincial research programs including National Natural Science Foundation of China grants and special talent programs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"工业场景因其制造环境半结构化、工况特征相对稳定、工艺流程相对标准，更易实现具身智能技术的快速落地，很有可能成为具身智能的首个规模化应用领域。" (Industrial scenarios, with their semi-structured environments, relatively stable operating conditions, and standardized processes, offer fertile ground for the swift deployment of embodied intelligence technologies and are poised to become the first domain to see their large-scale adoption.)
</key_excerpts>

This is a comprehensive Oracle Cloud Infrastructure article by Greg Pavlik (Senior Vice President, published February 11, 2025) explaining generative AI, its working principles, applications, benefits, risks, and future outlook.

### Definition and Key Concepts
- Generative AI (GenAI) is a subset of AI machine learning that creates new content (text, audio, images, video) in response to text prompts, based on training data inference rather than predefined rules.
- The modern GenAI wave began November 30, 2022, with the release of ChatGPT, built on OpenAI's GPT-3.5 neural network model. GPT stands for "Generative Pretrained Transformer."
- The first conversational chatbot, ELIZA, was developed at MIT in the mid-1960s but was rule-based and lacked contextual understanding.

### How It Works
- GenAI models use artificial neural networks (3D layers of artificial "neurons" with interconnected formulas and adjustable weights/parameters). GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters; GPT-4 reportedly has trillions (unverified).
- Models are trained by processing tokens (not words) and making predictions (e.g., next word in sequence). The backpropagation algorithm adjusts parameters after each prediction to improve accuracy.
- Fine-tuning uses techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which was used to create ChatGPT from GPT-3.5.
- **Key limitation:** Even AI experts cannot fully explain how models produce their outputs. Dean Thompson (former CTO of multiple AI startups acquired by LinkedIn and Yelp) notes the internal complexity of neural layers exceeds human analytical capacity.

### Business Impact and Statistics
- McKinsey evaluated 63 use cases across 16 business functions, concluding GenAI could generate trillions of dollars in value, with 75% coming from customer operations, marketing/sales, software engineering, and R&D.
- Gartner forecasts: by 2025, over 30% of new drugs and materials will be discovered using GenAI; 30% of outbound marketing messages will be synthetically generated (up from 2% in 2022); 38% of enterprises invest in GenAI for customer experience and retention.
- By 2024, 40% of enterprise applications include conversational AI; by 2026, over 100 million employees will collaborate with "machine colleagues."

### Applications and Use Cases
- Customer service: AI chatbots with multi-language support and real-time agent assistance

### Benefits
Five key advantages: improved productivity, lower costs, higher customer satisfaction, better decision-making, and accelerated product launches. These stem from knowledge synthesis, human-AI collaboration, and speed.

### Limitations and Risks
- **Hallucinations:** Models invent false information with equal confidence as real facts
- **Credibility/reliability:** Outdated training data and inaccuracies requiring human verification
- **Privacy/IP exposure:** Risk of leaking protected data or trade secrets
- **Social engineering:** Cybercriminals use GenAI for more convincing phishing attacks
- **Bias:** Training data bias reflected in outputs
- **Shadow AI:** Unapproved employee use leading to unintended consequences
- **Model collapse:** As AI-generated content proliferates, models trained on synthetic data may degrade in quality over time
- **Regulation:** Rapidly evolving AI regulations worldwide requiring compliance monitoring

## Embodied Intelligence for Flexible Manufacturing: A Survey

This is a comprehensive survey paper (published in 2025, Volume 47, Number 4) titled "Embodied Intelligence for Flexible Manufacturing: A Survey" (面向柔性制造的具身智能综述) by Chinese researchers from the National University of Defense Technology, Wuhan University, Shenzhen University, Hunan University, and Shenyang Institute of Automation (Chinese Academy of Sciences). Corresponding author: XU Kai (kevin.kai.xu@gmail.com).

### Core Thesis
Driven by recent breakthroughs in AI (e.g., DeepSeek, GPT-4), embodied intelligence is rapidly penetrating industrial manufacturing. Industrial scenarios—with semi-structured environments, stable operating conditions, and standardized processes—are poised to become the first domain for large-scale embodied intelligence adoption. However, the shift toward high-variety, small-batch flexible manufacturing (with mixed-model production lines, rapid product iterations, and non-standardized processes) presents three core challenges:
1. **Accurate process modeling and monitoring under limited sensing** (受限感知下的工艺精准建模监测)
2. **Dynamic balance between flexible adaptation and high-precision manipulation** (柔性适配与高精操控的动态平衡)
3. **Coordinating general robotic skills with specialized industrial procedures** (通用技能与专用工艺的协同融合)

### Framework: Industrial Eye-Hand-Brain (工业之眼-工业之手-工业之脑)
The survey organizes the field across three dimensions:
- **Industrial Eye (感知层)**: Multimodal data fusion and real-time modeling in complex dynamic environments
- **Industrial Hand (控制层)**: Flexible, adaptive, precise manipulation for demanding manufacturing processes
- **Industrial Brain (决策层)**: Intelligent optimization for process planning and line scheduling

The authors propose a **three-stage evolution model**: cognition enhancement → skill transition → system evolution (认知增强-技能跃迁-系统进化).

### Section 1: Industrial Eye
**1.1 3D Vision High-Precision Imaging**: Reviews three main 3D imaging methods—structured light (sub-millimeter accuracy, 0.1-5m range), Time-of-Flight (centimeter accuracy, 0.1-10m), and multi-view RGB (centimeter accuracy, 0.5-50m). Covers phase-measuring deflectometry (PMD) for high-reflectivity surfaces, line-scan cameras, KinectFusion, MIPS-Fusion, GeoTransformer for point cloud registration, NeRF, Gaussian Splatting, and emerging foundation models DUSt3R and VGGT. Case studies include automotive paint surface defect detection (reducing miss rates below 1% and false alarms below 3%) and shipbuilding non-structured welding scenarios (FoundationStereo achieving ±0.2mm depth reconstruction).

**1.2 Multi-source Data Fusion Sensing**: Covers feature extraction across modalities (RGB, depth/point clouds, acoustics, thermal infrared, force-torque), heterogeneous feature alignment via contrastive learning (CLIP), joint embedding, and attention mechanisms (MulT, AnyGPT, TEAL, Meta-Transformer). Describes early/middle/late fusion strategies. Case studies: Stanford's multi-modal (RGB-D + force-torque + proprioception) assembly using variational autoencoders with product of experts, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University's welding quality monitoring fusing vision, acoustic, and electrical signals using LSTM to predict defects 0-2 seconds in advance.

**1.3 Industrial Vision Foundation Models**: Reviews self-supervised learning approaches (masked image modeling, contrastive learning like SimCLR/MoCo/BYOL, teacher-student frameworks like DINO), SAM/SAM 2 for segmentation, Depth Anything, FoundationPose for 6D pose estimation, DINOv2, 3D-VisTA, DUSt3R, and VGGT. Covers fine-tuning methods (full fine-tuning, linear probing, PEFT including LoRA, Adapter Tuning, Prompt Tuning). Case studies: AnomalyDINO for few-shot defect detection using DINOv2 features, and DUSt3R for low-texture industrial image matching.

### Section 2: Industrial Hand
**2.1 Precise Control with Low-Precision Hardware**: Covers pose recognition (2D image-based like DOPE, SOCS; 3D-based like MIRETR), control strategy adaptation (traditional PID/LQR/fuzzy control vs. imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and hybrid IL+RL approaches like AMP and residual policies), and Sim2Real transfer (domain randomization, Gaussian splatting-based approaches like SplatSim, RobogSim, ManiGaussian, PIN-WM with physics-aware digital cousins). Case studies: Tsinghua's digital twin + residual policy for 3C product assembly (±0.05 to ±0.2mm tolerances), and Stanford's ALOHA system achieving millimeter-level precision on hardware costing under $20,000 (success rate improved from 60% to 96% for battery insertion and drill installation, with 30-40% shorter operation cycles).

**2.2 Flexible Operation on Reconfigurable Lines**: Covers general control policy learning (policy distillation like AutoMate achieving 86.5% success across 20 part types; meta-learning like ODA algorithm), interaction representation design (2D affordance-based approaches like VIMA, Instruct2Act; 3D representations like IBS-based grasping, DP3), and decision foundation models. Case study: University of Kentucky's data-driven arc welding real-time control converging pool width in just 7 control cycles.

### Section 3: Industrial Brain
**3.1 Factory Intelligent Scheduling**: Covers job shop scheduling (JSSP as NP-hard problem; traditional methods like branch-and-bound, genetic algorithms vs. learning-based approaches using GIN, multi-agent RL such as Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics' distributed scheduling system, LLM-based methods like SeEvo), autonomous mobile unit path planning (TSP/VRP formulations; RL and transformer approaches like AM, DIFUSCO, DISCO diffusion solvers), and material warehousing optimization (bin packing problem; deep RL methods like CDRL, PCT for online 3D packing). --- SOURCE 1: 焊接机器人离线编程系统的研究 ---
URL: https://hj.hwi.com.cn/cn/article/pdf/preview/10.12073/j.hj.20241126001.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, published in Welding & Joining (2025, Issue 8, pp. 52-60) by YIN Hao and CHEN Haiwei from Jiangnan University (Wuxi, China), describes the development of an off-line programming system for welding robots built on the SolidWorks platform using C# as the development tool. The system was designed to improve software versatility and off-line programming efficiency compared to traditional manual teaching methods.

KEY METHODOLOGY:
1. System architecture includes modules for: off-line programming environment, welding gun pose planning, inverse kinematics solving, motion simulation, reachability/collision detection, program generation, auxiliary functions, and welding parameter settings.
2. Weld seam selection is done through manual interaction, with feature analysis and information extraction.
3. Trajectory generation uses: straight-line interpolation for linear welds, three-point circular arc interpolation for circular welds (detected via ICurve::IsCircle()), and cubic polynomial interpolation with curve discretization (via ICurve::GetTessPts()) for complex intersecting-curve (相贯线) welds.
4. Initial welding gun attitude planning uses two methods: the perpendicular method (垂线法) for regular orthogonal cylindrical welds where welding work angle (α) and travel angle (β) are pre-input by users, and the normal vector orthogonal method (法向量正交法) for irregular intersecting pipes where attitudes are determined entirely by the two intersecting surface normal vectors. For interpolation points not simultaneously on both surfaces, a "secondary point" (nearest point on the other surface) is used.
5. Attitude interpolation in neighborhood intervals uses unit quaternion spherical linear interpolation (Slerp) when users manually adjust individual welding gun attitudes, handling two edge cases: quaternion dot product < 0 (taking the negation to avoid long-way interpolation on the 4D sphere) and very small angles (using linear approximation).
6. Robot kinematics uses improved D-H parameter method with Pieper criterion for inverse solutions (matching TCP calibration values: l1=52.83mm, l2=324.68mm, θ=31°).

KEY RESULTS:
- The welding experiment used a three-way exhaust pipe (saddle-shaped weld) made of 304 stainless steel (3mm thick), with arc start/stop time of 0.6s.
- Comparison of trajectory discretization accuracy: 6mm vs 3mm settings (weld width 6mm) showed that higher discretization accuracy (3mm) produced more uniform, continuous weld beads with evenly distributed fish-scale patterns and no defects like weld build-up or undercut.
- The robot moved smoothly in real welding scenarios with no singular positions, angle overruns, or collisions.
- The system ensures smooth welding gun movement and improves welding quality, offering high versatility for arbitrary complex models and significantly improving off-line programming efficiency for automated and intelligent welding production.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"该系统以人工交互的方式选择焊缝，并对焊缝进行特征分析及信息提取；依据焊缝形状采用直线、圆弧插补算法或三次多项式插值法拟合生成焊接轨迹" (The system selects weld seams through manual interaction, analyzes characteristics and extracts information; uses straight line, circular interpolation or cubic polynomial interpolation to generate welding trajectories based on weld shape)

--- SOURCE 2: Research on multi-robot collaborative welding for large and complex structures of ships ---
URL: https://html.rhhz.net/jckxjsgw/html/73756.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper titled "Research on multi-robot collaborative welding for large and complex structures of ships" by Qian Tian-long (Cosco Shipping Heavy Industry, Yangzhou, China) and You Rui-chao (Tangshan Kaiyuan Autowelding System Co., Ltd., Tangshan, China), published in *Ship Science and Technology* (舰船科学技术), 2024, Vol. 46, Issue 5, pages 39-42 (DOI: 10.3404/j.issn.1672-7649.2024.05.007). The paper was received on November 9, 2023, and funded by a Ministry of Industry and Information Technology project (Z2301E01).

**Methodology:**
1. Constructed a welding dynamic force balance equation for multiple welding robots (master-slave collaborative control mode with one master and multiple slave robots).
2. Set constraint conditions (robot posture, acceleration/speed limits, collision avoidance) and established a welding planning model with two optimization objectives: minimizing total welding completion time (J1) and maximizing welding task balance (J2).
3. Used a region division method to partition ship welding points into zones.
4. Applied meta-heuristic nested algorithms to design multi-robot collaborative welding planning.
5. Used a fractional-order PID controller, converting the welding control transfer function into an integer-order transfer function via the Oustaloup filter, enabling precise tracking of target weld seams and output of ideal welding trajectories.

**Experimental Setup and Results:**
- The experiment used the 100Q10 large ship model with 4 Kuka KR18 welding robots (18 kg payload, 6 axes, ±0.1mm repeatability, 400V welder voltage, 5-500A welder current).
- Total of 153 welding process points were distributed across four robots (35, 42, 37, and 39 points respectively).
- Welding completion times were 16, 18, 15, and 14 minutes respectively, with total completion time of 18 minutes.
- Task balance values were 0.945, 0.937, 0.915, and 0.942 per robot, with an overall balance of 0.935.
- Actual weld trajectories from the robots closely matched ideal trajectories, validating the fractional-order PID controller's precision.

**Conclusions:** The proposed multi-robot collaborative welding technology effectively balances welding tasks among robots, improves welding efficiency and quality, and supports the automation and intelligent development of shipbuilding welding. The paper references 8 prior studies on multi-robot path planning, welding robot tracking, offline programming, and related topics.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The experimental results show that the overall balance of welding tasks executed using this technology is as high as 0.935, which has good application effects."
</key_excerpts>

<summary>
This is a comprehensive Chinese-language guide from Spatial (blog.spatial.com) about Robot Offline Programming (OLP) for industrial robots. Published 09-04-2026 by the Spatial Team, the article explains how offline programming is replacing traditional teach pendant methods and details the complete OLP software workflow.

**Key topics covered:**

1. **Why OLP is replacing traditional teach pendant programming**: Traditional online programming requires technicians to manually guide robot arms (up to 200kg) inside safety cages using teach pendants. This causes production downtime, exposes workers to danger zones, and yields zero output during programming. For complex tasks like automotive body welding with hundreds of Tool Center Points (TCP), this process is extremely painful. OLP solves all three problems by using virtual digital twin models on computers to write, test, and verify programs without stopping production.

2. **The 7-step OLP workflow**: (1) Import CAD data via 3D InterOp, (2) Layout the workstation, (3) Generate TCPs based on surface normals and edge geometry, (4) Motion simulation with collision and reachability checks, (5) Generate native robot code for ABB, KUKA, FANUC controllers, (6) On-machine debugging with minor tuning, (7) Full-speed production.

3. **Spatial's 3D CAD technology stack for OLP**:
   - **3D InterOp**: Reads CATIA, NX, SolidWorks, Creo, and Inventor formats without requiring licenses. Preserves geometry, topology, PMI, and metadata. B-Rep accuracy is critical because surface normals drive TCP placement.
   - **CGM Modeler**: Provides programmatic surface normal queries for precise tool positioning and arc-length parameterization for uniform sampling along curves. Supports smooth edge propagation for G1 continuous motion.
   - **Spatial AGM SpaCD (collision detection)**: Offers real-time continuous detection and comprehensive pre-verification with all collision pairs and intersected geometry. Includes safety clearance proactive detection and parallel architecture supporting thousands of collision checks per second.
   - **HOOPS Visualize**: Standard rendering layer for high-end 3D robot simulation software, handling massive triangle meshes with fluid interactive animation.
   - **Data simplification and boundary volumes**: CGM polyhedra for discrete mesh representations and AABB hierarchies for fast collision rejection.

4. **Path planning in robotics**: Explained as the challenge of finding collision-free joint configurations between start and target states under kinematic and mechanical constraints. Key components include configuration space, mechanical constraints, motion models, and inverse kinematics (IK). Practical engineering techniques include warm-starting, smoothing, and target-region vs. target-point planning. Spatial's path planning solvers (in CDS and AGM framework) handle IK, 2D/3D constraint management, and dynamic simulation, with specialized solvers for Universal Robots, KUKA, Yaskawa, and Techman Robot series.

5. **Intelligent diagnostics**: Good path planners should explain failures - distinguishing between reachability issues, singularities, and tight clearance constraints. This is particularly important for non-expert manufacturing engineers.

6. **Real-world applications driving path planning demand**: Car body inspection, arc/spot welding, deburring, dual-arm robot systems (solving two 6-DOF chains simultaneously), and gantry systems.

7. **Competitive landscape**: Siemens' KineoWorks is a mature reference implementation but expensive. Staubli evaluated KineoWorks and found it poor value, switching to Spatial's component stack. The AGM framework integrates HOOPS Visualize, SpaCD, CDS, InterOp, and CGM under a single application development framework.

8. **Customer list**: ABB, Staubli, Yaskawa, Daisen, Nachi, Kawasaki, and Fanuc all use Spatial components for production robot offline programming software. ABB built RobotStudio on this workflow, and Staubli developed its Robotics Suite 2022.
</summary>

"机器人离线编程，是指在电脑上，利用物理机器人工作站的虚拟数字孪生模型，完成机器人运动程序的编写、测试与验证，全程不停止生产、不进入作业现场。机器人继续执行当前任务，工程师在仿真中开发下一套程序。", "机器人行业的发展前景令人振奋。机器人是最灵活的自动化生产设备。与 Spatial 合作意味着与 3D 环境领域的领导者合作，这让我们对为客户提供的解决方案更有信心。——史陶比尔机器人公司市场经理", "可操作的诊断功能将有用的离线机器人编程软件与只显示红色并让编程人员猜测的工具区分开来。这对于非专业用户（即了解物理过程但不是机器人专家的制造工程师）来说尤为重要。", "Spatial 的文档说得很清楚：\"如果不是 Spatial，客户就必须将问题一个个分开。这是一项耗时的工作。\"", "史陶比尔为其机器人套件评估了 KineoWorks，发现其性价比并不适合他们的使用案例，因此他们转而使用 Spatial 的组件堆栈。Spatial 的路径规划求解器是一个有能力的替代方案。"

--- SOURCE 17: 机械加工工艺开发智能方法研究 - 零部件制造 - AI汽车网 ---
URL: https://auto.jgvogel.cn/c1498790.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published by "AI汽车制造业" on March 25, 2025, and authored by 张云飞 (Zhang Yunfei) of 上汽通用动力科技（上海）有限公司 (SAIC-GM Powertrain Technology, Shanghai), presents an intelligent method for mechanical machining process development based on Model-Based Definition (MBD) technology combined with intelligent algorithms.

**Research Background and Context:**
The paper notes that most manufacturing enterprises in China still rely on traditional Computer-Aided Process Planning (CAPP) systems, which have limitations as Industry 4.0 and intelligent manufacturing continue to advance. The research demonstrates how MBD technology enables automatic extraction of Product Manufacturing Information (PMI) from 3D product models, significantly improving the efficiency and accuracy of converting product information to process information.

**Key Technical Route (4 Modules):**

1. **Product Information Recognition and Extraction**: Uses MBD technology to automatically identify and extract geometric features and process requirements from 3D models. This involves building a feature rule library (covering holes, slots, keys, bosses, etc.), developing feature recognition algorithms, extracting PMI information (dimensions, form/position tolerances, surface roughness), and generating structured feature attribute data readable by both machines and engineers.

2. **Intelligent Process Method Reasoning**: Based on a structured knowledge base and inference algorithms. Includes building a process knowledge database (rules, parameters, cases, experience), using "IF-THEN" rule-based reasoning for 常规 operations plus case-based reasoning to derive solutions for similar problems, generating machining plans, tool selection, and processing parameters. A platform-based inference engine is integrated into a cloud platform.

3. **Intelligent Process Route Orchestration**: Uses optimization algorithms (operations research, regional optimization, and shortest-path algorithms) to generate optimal process routes. The planning process is formulated as a large-scale mixed-integer programming (MIP) problem. The module includes data preprocessing, branch-and-bound pruning for infeasible solutions, application of Hamiltonian cycle theory for conflict pre-checking, and divides machining regions before optimizing each region and integrating results via shortest-path algorithms.

4. **Automated Process Document Generation**: Automatically generates standardized process documents including process flow charts, control plans, PFMEA, and tool lists using standardized templates. A management platform supports online concurrent generation, version management, approval workflows, and precise/fuzzy searching of process document databases.

**International Examples Cited:**
- Boeing 777 used MBD technology entirely for 3D digital product definition, digital assembly, and digital machining process planning, reducing development cycle time by 50%, reducing rework rates by 75%, and cutting costs by 25%.
- ASME developed the ASME Y14.41 "Digital Product Definition Data Practices" standard with Boeing's assistance.
- MBD applications in Chinese shipbuilding and aerospace industries have improved manufacturing efficiency and enabled 3D visualization of processes.

**Validation Results:**
- Initially piloted in engine projects, then expanded to transmissions, electric drives, and eventually all machining projects within the company's powertrain division.
- Successfully applied to more than 10 powertrain projects.
- Process planning time reduced by 75% compared to traditional methods.
- Tool cost (Cost Per Unit) significantly reduced across all projects over the past 3 years.
- Data consistency achieved at 100%.
- The application promoted innovation in process planning operational modes for more efficient and precise workflows.

**Conclusion:**
The intelligent machining process development model, covering the four key steps from product information extraction to process document generation, has been widely validated in actual production. It demonstrates significant advancement in systematization, automation, and intelligence. The hybrid business-algorithm model has strong scalability and can be extended to the entire machining field through database updates.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Chinese academic research article titled "具身智能驱动的智能制造应用发展研究" (Development of Intelligent Manufacturing Driven by Embodied Intelligence), published in the journal 中国工程科学 (Strategic Study of CAE) in 2025, Vol. 27, Issue 3, pages 67-82. Authors: 袁依格, 何卓丰, 李威, 胡东滨 (corresponding author), affiliated with Xiangjiang Laboratory (Changsha 410205) and Business School of Central South University (Changsha 410083). The paper was received on 2025-04-15 and published on 2025-06-22.

KEY CONTENT:

**1. Introduction**: The paper explores embodied intelligence applications in intelligent manufacturing to support the transformation and high-quality development of China's manufacturing industry. Embodied intelligence combines AI and robotics to give machines a "perception-decision-execution" closed loop, enabling adaptive learning, collaborative operation, and flexibility in complex manufacturing environments.

**2. Technical Evolution of Intelligent Manufacturing** (three stages):
- **Rule-based automated manufacturing**: Uses PLCs, CNC machines, and SCADA systems for pre-programmed operations (e.g., GERBERcutter S-70, KUKA welding systems). Limitations include lack of flexibility and self-learning capability.
- **Data-driven digital intelligent manufacturing**: Uses sensor networks, industrial internet, cloud computing, big data analytics, and AI for real-time monitoring and optimization (e.g., Sany Group's smart factory, Beijing Benz's big data platform, digital twin systems). Still lacks higher-level autonomous cognition.
- **Embodied-intelligence-enabled manufacturing**: Gives machines human-like cognitive abilities for perception, understanding, learning, and decision-making. Examples: 墨现科技's finger pressure sensors (96 sensing points, 3.5g trigger force), 优必选's Walker S humanoid robots in NEV factories, Huawei's automated production lines.

**3. Technical System** (three dimensions):
- **Interaction model**: "Perception-Decision-Execution-Feedback" closed loop involving humans, machines, and environment.
- **Key technical elements**: (a) Multimodal manufacturing data fusion perception (data-level, feature-level, and target-level fusion); (b) Embodied intelligence manufacturing powered by foundation models (using transformer-based multimodal encoders, knowledge graphs, GPT-4 for autonomous robot task execution); (c) Force control technology (force sensing, feedback control via impedance/compliance control, behavior planning, intelligent optimization); (d) Robot motion planning algorithms (RRT, A* algorithms, deep reinforcement learning for path planning and trajectory generation).
- **Technical framework**: Seven layers - physical layer, data layer, algorithm layer, perception layer, decision layer, execution layer, and feedback layer.

**4. Empowering Functions**:
- Revolutionizes production (e.g., 中原动力's embodied AI in electrolytic aluminum carbon block polishing, 常州微亿智造's rapid line debugging from one week to hours, humanoid robots for dangerous painting tasks)
- Upgrades warehousing and logistics (intelligent storage robots, AGVs, autonomous delivery vehicles)
- Ensures inspection and maintenance (predictive maintenance, e.g., 优艾智合's intelligent O&M model at Bohai oil field; robots for nuclear plants and deep-sea platforms)
- Enhances human-robot collaboration (Industry 5.0 human-centered manufacturing, multimodal sensor-equipped robotic arms, brain-computer interfaces)

**5. Application Challenges** (five major difficulties):
1. Lack of multimodal data limiting practical effectiveness
2. Complex manufacturing environments increasing perception difficulty (uneven lighting, dust, electromagnetic noise, vibration)
3. AI hallucinations causing safety risks (errors in perception, decision, and execution phases)
4. Software-hardware integration problems (compatibility gaps, interface standardization issues, timing synchronization challenges)
5. Missing ethical and legal standards creating compliance challenges

**6. Development Trends**:
- Expanding application scenarios (from traditional manufacturing to high-end equipment, new energy, aerospace, medical health)
- Deeper human-robot collaboration
- Increasingly mature industrial ecosystem

**7. Recommendations**:
- Strengthen technical research to overcome key bottlenecks
- Improve the industrial ecosystem to promote application deployment
- Establish standards and regulations to ensure production safety
- Expand application scenarios to open market opportunities (aviation, aerospace, automotive, high-end equipment, new energy, electronics)

**Funding**: Chinese Academy of Engineering consulting project "全球未来产业发展趋势及湖南未来产业布局研究" (2024-DFZD-39) and Xiangjiang Laboratory project (24XJ01002).

The paper includes 60 references covering Chinese and English academic literature on intelligent manufacturing, embodied intelligence, robotics, AI, and related technologies.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: 《世界机器人2025》报告：全球工业机器人发展格局 ---
URL: https://www.istis.sh.cn/cms/news/article/75/27784

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage reports on the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) "World Robotics 2025" report, released on September 25, 2025, which analyzes the global industrial robot market landscape. Key findings include:

**Global Overview:**
- In 2024, global new industrial robot installations reached 542,000 units, more than double the figure from 10 years ago. This marks the fourth consecutive year of exceeding 500,000 annual installations.
- Asia accounted for 74% of global new installations in 2024, with Europe at 16% and the Americas at 9%.
- The total global operational stock of industrial robots reached 4.664 million units in 2024, up 9% year-over-year.
- 2024's annual installation figure was the second-highest in history, only 2% below the peak two years prior.

**Asia:**
- China remained the world's largest industrial robot market, accounting for 54% of global new installations (295,000 units in 2024, a record high). For the first time, domestic Chinese manufacturers outsold foreign suppliers in the domestic market, with local brands' domestic market share jumping from ~28% over the past decade to 57% in 2024. China's operational robot stock surpassed 2 million units, the largest of any country. Chinese manufacturing robot demand is expected to grow at an average of 10% annually through 2028.
- Japan remained the second-largest market with 44,500 new installations in 2024 (down 4%), with operational stock of 450,500 units (up 3%). Japan's robot demand is expected to grow at low single-digit rates in 2025.
- South Korea installed 30,600 units in 2024 (down 3%), ranking as the world's fourth-largest market.
- India set a record with 9,100 installations (up 7%), driven primarily by the automotive sector (45% market share). India ranked sixth globally.

**Europe:**
- European installations fell 8% to 85,000 units in 2024 (still the second-highest historically). 80% of European installations (67,800 units) occurred within the EU. European demand benefited from nearshoring trends, with 3% average annual growth from 2019-2024.
- Germany was Europe's largest and globally fifth-largest market with 26,982 installations (down 5%), representing 32% of Europe's total.
- Italy: 8,783 installations (down 16%); Spain: 5,100 (third in Europe, strong automotive demand); France: 4,900 (down 24%, fell to fourth); UK: 2,500 (down 35%, 19th globally). The UK's 2023 record of 3,800 was a one-time peak driven by a "super deduction" tax credit program that ended in Q1 2023.

**Americas:**
- The Americas exceeded 50,000 installations for the fourth consecutive year with 50,100 units in 2024 (down 10%).
- The US was the region's largest market, accounting for 68% of installations with 34,200 units (down 9%). The US imports most robots from Japan and Europe but has many domestic system integrators.
- Mexico: 5,600 installations (down 4%), with automotive industry accounting for 63% of installations.

The study was funded by the National Social Science Fund General Project (22BJL049) and the Wuhan Social Science Fund Later-stage Project (2024026).

**Research Objective and Methodology:** The study examines whether and how China's Intelligent Manufacturing Pilot Demonstration Projects affect enterprises' "new quality productive forces" (新质生产力), a concept representing the Chinese innovation of Marxist productive forces theory combining technological advancement with management innovation. Using panel data from 15,511 observations of Chinese manufacturing A-share listed companies from 2011-2022, the authors employ a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) design. They construct four complementary measures of new quality productive forces: (1) an entropy-weight method index, (2) a Word2Vec neural network model-based text measure using analyst reports, (3) relative total factor productivity changes within industries, and (4) a proxy based on labor and production tools.

**Key Findings:**
- Intelligent manufacturing policy significantly enhances enterprise new quality productive forces, with coefficients significant at 1% or 5% levels across all four measurement methods (e.g., coefficient of 0.093 for NQPF measure).
- Results remain robust after PSM, entropy balancing, instrumental variable estimation (using 2003 city-level IT employment and terrain ruggedness as instruments), two-stage DID, Heckman two-stage models, double machine learning (random forest, Lasso, ridge regression, SVM), placebo tests (1,000 random iterations), and exclusion of competing policies (AI innovation pilot zones, smart city pilots, Broadband China, digital government construction, national big data pilot zones).

**Mechanisms (Hypothesis 2 validated):** The policy operates through three channels:
1. **Promoting enterprise basic research**: Increased R&D subsidies, reduced financing constraints, enhanced collaborative research with universities/institutes, and breakthroughs in core technologies.
2. **Facilitating intelligent production transformation**: Significant growth in intelligent equipment investment, increased industrial robot penetration, improved production flexibility, and higher capacity utilization.
3. **Optimizing labor structure**: Increased demand for AI-related positions and high-tech talent, higher proportions of skilled workers, and workforce restructuring toward high-skill roles.

**Heterogeneity Findings:**
- Effect is significant only for high-tech enterprises, not non-high-tech firms.
- Significant for technology-intensive and labor-intensive industries, but not for capital-intensive industries.
- Stronger effects in regions with higher intellectual property protection levels.
- Positive spillover effects on downstream enterprises' new quality productive forces, but no significant effect on upstream enterprises.

**Policy Context:** China's intelligent manufacturing policy evolved from the 2006 inclusion of "intelligent manufacturing" in national science strategy, through "Made in China 2025" (2015) and the "Intelligent Manufacturing Development Plan (2016-2020)." The pilot projects progressed from smart factory construction (2015) to cross-industry standard promotion (2016-2017) and industrial cluster intelligent upgrades (2018 onward).

**Policy Recommendations (six total):** Expand intelligent manufacturing pilot coverage with evaluation mechanisms; strengthen enterprise basic research and technology transfer; increase digital-intelligent investment through dedicated policy funds and diversified financing; release intelligent human capital dividends through skill training and targeted subsidies; differentiate policy implementation by enterprise type and strengthen IP protection; and build a whole industrial chain collaborative intelligent transformation support system with a dedicated industry chain development fund.

**Core Thesis and Contributions:**
- Embodied intelligence is rapidly penetrating industrial manufacturing due to advances in AI (DeepSeek, GPT-4). Industrial scenarios—with semi-structured environments, stable conditions, and standardized processes—are poised to be the first domain for large-scale embodied intelligence adoption.
- The shift toward high-productivity, small-batch flexible manufacturing creates new normal conditions: mixed-model production lines, rapid product iterations, and unstructured non-standard processes. This poses three core challenges: (1) accurate process modeling/monitoring under limited sensing, (2) maintaining dynamic balance between flexible adaptation and high-precision manipulation, and (3) coordinating general robotic skills with specialized industrial procedures.

**Organizing Framework — "Industrial Eye - Industrial Hand - Industrial Brain" (工业之眼-工业之手-工业之脑):**

**Part 1: Industrial Eye (Perception Layer)** covers multimodal data fusion and real-time modeling:
- 3D vision high-precision imaging: structured light (sub-millimeter precision, 0.1-5m range), Time-of-Flight (cm-level precision, 0.1-10m), and multi-view RGB imaging (cm-level, 0.5-50m). Methods include Fourier Transform Profilometry, Phase-Shifting Profilometry, Phase Measuring Deflectometry (for high-reflection surfaces), line-scan cameras, KinectFusion, MIPS-Fusion, GeoTransformer, COLMAP, NeRF, Gaussian Splatting, and emerging foundation models DUSt3R and VGGT.
- Defect detection and dimensional measurement: 3D vision enables micro-meter to sub-millimeter precision (e.g., ±0.2mm non-contact measurement, reconstruction error <0.05mm for complex engine housings). Case studies include automotive paint surface reconstruction via PMD (reducing false-negative rates to <1%, false-positive to <3%) and ship welding with FoundationStereo achieving ±0.2mm depth reconstruction.
- Multi-source data fusion: covers RGB, depth/point cloud, acoustic, infrared, and force-torque modalities. Feature extraction uses ResNet, ViT, PointNet++, Point Transformer, 1D CNN, TCN, GRU. Pretrained models (MAE, DINOv2, PointMAE, PTv3, PANNs, TimesNet) reduce training costs. Alignment via contrastive learning (CLIP), joint embedding, and attention mechanisms (MulT, EMT, AnyGPT, TEAL, Meta-Transformer). Fusion strategies include early, late, and intermediate fusion with trade-offs.
- Industrial vision foundation models: self-supervised learning (MIM, contrastive learning, teacher-student frameworks like DINO), SAM/SAM 2 for segmentation, Depth Anything for depth estimation, FoundationPose for 6D pose, 3D-VisTA and UniT3D for 3D tasks. Fine-tuning via full fine-tuning, linear probing, and PEFT (LoRA, Adapter Tuning, Prompt Tuning). Case studies include AnomalyDINO for few-shot defect detection and DUSt3R for low-texture image matching.

**Part 2: Industrial Hand (Control Layer)** covers flexible adaptive precise manipulation:
- Low-precision hardware control: pose recognition (DOPE, SOCS, MIRETR for cluttered scenes), control strategies comparing traditional model-driven (PID, LQR, fuzzy logic), imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and IL+RL hybrids (Deepmimic, AMP, residual policies). Sim2Real transfer via domain randomization, Gaussian Splatting (SplatSim, RobogSim, ManiGaussian, PIN-WM). Case studies: Tsinghua's digital-twin + residual policy for 3C assembly, and Stanford's ALOHA system achieving millimeter-level dual-arm manipulation on <$20K hardware (success rate improved from 60% to 96%, cycle time reduced 30-40%).

Case studies: NVIDIA's universal assembly policy and RoboGrind LLM-guided grinding system.

**Part 3: Industrial Brain (Decision Layer)** covers process planning and line scheduling:
- Factory scheduling: Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP) via traditional methods (branch-and-bound, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, tabu search) and learning-based approaches (GIN-based reinforcement learning, multi-agent RL with PPO, LLM-based auto algorithm design like SeEvo). Multi-AGV path planning (TSP/VRP) using RL, transformer attention (AM), and diffusion solvers (DIFUSCO, DISCO). Online bin packing via deep RL (CDRL, PCT for continuous 3D online packing, TAP-Net for joint order and position optimization).
- Digital twin for virtual-physical synchronization: state perception, synchronization, and twin-based intelligent scheduling for enhanced flexibility and responsiveness.

**Key Challenges and Data Points:**
- Assembly precision requirements: ±0.05mm (auto assembly), 0.1-0.5mm gaps; grinding: Ra ≤0.8μm, shape error ±0.2mm (wind blades), ±0.03mm (aero-engine blades); welding: ±0.2 to ±0.5mm standard tracking, ±0.1-0.2mm for precision applications.

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
* [首页](https://www.zdsztech.com/blog/)
* [知识百科](https://www.zdsztech.com/blog/docs/)
* 详情

2,189

## 一、定义与核心特征：一张图看懂离散制造与流程制造

**离散制造（Discrete Manufacturing）**：指通过对独立的零部件进行加工、装配，最终生产出具有明确功能和独立形态的产品。其生产过程在物理或化学上是可逆、可拆解的。

**流程制造（Process Manufacturing）**：指通过混合、分离、化合或一系列化学反应，将原材料转化为产品的生产方式。其生产过程通常是不可逆的，产品一旦形成便难以分解回原始物料。

| 对比维度 | 离散制造 | 流程制造 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **生产对象 (产品形态)** | 固定的、可计数的单元（个、件、台），形态稳定，可拆分和重装。 | 连续的、不可分割的物料（吨、升、批），形态可能在生产中改变（液体、粉末、气体）。 |
| **生产过程 (工艺路线)** | 工艺路线多变、不固定，常有返工、跳转，生产路径复杂。 | 工艺路线相对固定、连续，通常按预设顺序进行，中断成本高。 |
| **生产订单 (批量与连续性)** | 以“批次”或“订单”为单位组织生产，批量大小灵活，可按需生产。 | 通常是连续或大批量生产，以“期间”或“产能”为导向。 |
| **核心管理重点** | **物料清单（BOM）**。管理复杂的零部件层级关系、物料替代和工程变更。 | **配方（Formula/Recipe）**。管理原材料的精确配比、活性成分、产出率和联/副产品。 |
| **典型行业举例** | 汽车、电子、机械设备、家具、航空航天。 | 石油化工、制药、食品饮料、钢铁冶金、精细化工。 |

---

> * **左侧：离散制造** - 图标：齿轮与螺丝刀。关键词：**BOM、装配、工单、可拆卸**。流程图：多条分支、可回溯的箭头指向一个最终产品（如汽车）。
> * **右侧：流程制造** - 图标：烧杯与管道。关键词：**配方、反应、连续流、不可逆**。流程图：一条从原材料输入到管道混合、反应，最终流出产品的线性流程（如瓶装饮料）。

---

## 二、关键区别深度剖析：从生产到管理的5大差异

* **物料管理与BOM结构 vs. 配方管理**离散制造的核心是物料清单（BOM），它以树状结构精确描述了从成品、半成品到原材料的层级关系。一个复杂产品（如一部手机）的BOM可能包含数千个物料，管理重点在于版本控制、工程变更（ECN）和物料替代。而流程制造的核心是配方（Formula），它定义了原材料的精确百分比或数量，并关注活性成分、批次特性、产出率以及联产品（Co-products）和副产品（By-products）的管理。例如，在制药中，同一原料药的不同批次可能因活性成分差异而需要调整配方。
* **成本核算方式：分批成本法 vs. 分步成本法**由于生产以订单为驱动，离散制造普遍采用**分批成本法**（Job Order Costing）。成本核算对象是每一张生产订单或批次，将直接材料、直接人工和制造费用归集到特定的订单上，核算单个产品的成本相对清晰。流程制造则多采用**分步成本法**（Process Costing），将成本归集到生产步骤或部门（如混合、反应、灌装），再将总成本按产量平均分配到单位产品上，更关注单位时间内的平均成本。
* **质量控制节点：零部件检验 vs. 过程参数监控**离散制造的质量控制重点在于**零部件检验（IQC）、过程检验（IPQC）和成品检验（FQC）**。质量追溯可以精确到某个零件的批次和供应商。而在流程制造中，质量是在生产过程中形成的，因此重点在于对**关键过程参数（如温度、压力、pH值、流速）的实时监控（SPC）**。一旦过程参数偏离，整批产品都可能报废。其质量追溯更关注生产批次、环境数据和操作记录。
* **计划与排程逻辑：基于订单的排程 vs. 基于产能的连续计划**离散制造的生产计划与排程（APS）系统需要处理复杂的约束，如设备、模具、人员技能等，目标是在满足交期的前提下，实现设备利用率最大化和在制品最小化，其逻辑是**基于订单的有限能力排程**。流程制造的计划则更侧重于**基于产能和市场需求的连续生产计划**，需要考虑设备清场时间、储罐容量、管道切换等因素，目标是最大化设备运行时间，减少昂贵的停机和切换。
* **设备维护策略：单点故障影响 vs. 连续生产线维护**在离散制造车间，一台设备的故障通常只会影响单个工序，可以通过调整工艺路线或调度来规避，影响范围相对可控。因此，设备维护策略（EAM）可以更加灵活。但在流程制造中，生产线是高度耦合的，任何一个关键设备的非计划停机都可能导致整条生产线停摆，造成巨大的产量损失。因此，其设备维护策略更强调**预测性维护和预防性维护**，以保障生产的连续性和稳定性。

## 三、数字化系统选型指南：不同制造模式下的管理软件需求

上述差异直接决定了企业在选择MES、ERP等管理软件时，必须关注其功能是否与自身的生产模式相匹配。一个为离散行业设计的标准ERP，在流程行业可能会“水土不服”。下表清晰对比了两种模式对软件核心功能的不同要求：

| 核心功能 | 离散型MES/ERP | 流程型MES/ERP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **生产建模** | 侧重于\*\*工作中心、工艺路线（Routing）和物料清单（BOM）\*\*的管理。 | 侧重于**资源（设备、管道）、配方（Formula/Recipe）和生产流程**的建模。 |
| **车间排程** | 支持复杂的**工序级排程**，考虑模具、工装、人员等多种约束。 | 支持**基于设备产能的连续排程**，考虑储罐容量、切换时间、批次排序。 |

汽车制造是典型的**离散制造**。整个过程涉及将数万个独立的零部件（如发动机、底盘、车门、电子元件）通过冲压、焊装、涂装、总装等一系列明确的工序，组装成一辆完整的汽车。其生产过程是可拆解的，以“台”为单位进行管理，并且高度依赖复杂的物料清单（BOM）和精细的生产排程。

### 2. 如何判断我的公司是混合型制造？

This webpage from zdsztech.com provides a comprehensive comparison between discrete manufacturing (离散制造) and process manufacturing (流程制造), serving as an educational guide for businesses to understand their manufacturing models and select appropriate digital management systems.

**Key Definitions:**
- **Discrete Manufacturing**: Processing and assembling independent components into products with clear functions and independent forms. The production process is reversible and disassemblable.
- **Process Manufacturing**: Converting raw materials into products through mixing, separation, compounding, or chemical reactions. The process is typically irreversible.

**Five Key Differences (comparison table included):**
1. **Product form**: Discrete = countable fixed units (pieces, units); Process = continuous indivisible materials (tons, liters, batches)
2. **Production process**: Discrete = variable, complex routes with rework/jumps; Process = fixed, continuous routes where interruption is costly
3. **Production orders**: Discrete = batch/order-driven with flexible lot sizes; Process = continuous or large-batch, capacity-oriented
4. **Core management focus**: Discrete = BOM (bill of materials) management; Process = Formula/Recipe management (precise ratios, active ingredients, yield rates)
5. **Typical industries**: Discrete = automotive, electronics, machinery, furniture, aerospace; Process = petrochemical, pharmaceuticals, food & beverage, steel/metallurgy, fine chemicals

**Five Deep-Dive Differences:**
1. **Material management**: BOM tree structures with version control and engineering changes (discrete) vs. formula/recipe management focusing on active ingredients, batch properties, co-products and by-products (process)
2. **Cost accounting**: Job order costing (discrete) vs. process costing (process)
3. **Quality control**: Component inspection (IQC/IPQC/FQC) with batch/supplier traceability (discrete) vs. real-time monitoring of process parameters like temperature, pressure, pH, flow rate using SPC (process)
4. **Planning & scheduling**: Order-based finite capacity scheduling (discrete) vs. capacity and market demand-based continuous production planning considering equipment cleaning time and tank capacity (process)
5. **Equipment maintenance**: Single-point failure has limited impact (discrete) vs. highly coupled production lines where any unplanned downtime stops the entire line, requiring predictive and preventive maintenance (process)

**Software Selection Guide:** The page compares how discrete vs. process MES/ERP systems differ across production modeling, workshop scheduling, data collection, quality traceability, and inventory management. For example, discrete systems focus on work centers, routing and BOM, while process systems focus on resources, formulas/recipes and continuous scheduling.

**Future Trend - Hybrid Manufacturing:** Many industries increasingly combine both models (e.g., pharmaceuticals: API synthesis is process, tableting/packaging is discrete; food: beverage production is process, bottling/packing is discrete). Traditional rigid software struggles with hybrid models. The article positions no-code platforms (specifically the "支道平台" / Zhidao platform) as the solution, offering process engines, form engines and rule engines that allow companies to build customized MES, QMS, or ERP modules that handle both discrete and process characteristics. Claims include implementation cycles shortened by 2x+ and total costs reduced by 50-80% compared to traditional development.

**FAQ Highlights:**
- Automotive manufacturing is a typical discrete manufacturing process
- A "form transformation point" in production indicates hybrid manufacturing
- Using standard ERP in process industries risks recipe management gaps, distorted cost accounting, difficult quality traceability, and unit conversion chaos
- No-code platforms offer personalization, rapid iteration, integration across MES/QMS/WMS/ERP, and 50-80% cost reduction

The page also promotes Zhidao platform's ten business scenario solutions (production manufacturing, engineering services, sales/trade, inventory, production management, customer management, project management, contracts/accounts, HR, and after-sales).

行业动态

## 非标自动化设备夹具的设计制造

发布日期：2023.03.04 浏览次数（4667）

一、非标自动化设备夹具结构和夹紧力的设计

1、夹具结构设计要点：

（1）能保证工件定位后占据正确位置。

（2）要保证工件在整个加工过程中的位置稳定不变，振动小，又要使工件不产生过大的夹紧变形。

（3）夹紧装置的复杂程度与生产类型相适应。工件的生产批量越大，允许设计越复杂、效率越高的夹紧装置。

（4）工艺性好，使用性好。其结构应尽量简单，便于制造和维修；尽可能使用标准夹具零部件。

二、非标自动化设备夹具的整体刚度设计

夹具不同于其他环节，他在工艺系统中有着特殊地位，夹具的整体刚度对工件加工的动态误差产生着非常特殊的影响。当夹具的整体刚度远大于其他环节，工件加工的动态误差基本上只取决于夹具的制造精度和安装精度。因此设计夹具时，对夹具的整体刚度应给予足够重视。如因工艺系统其他环节的刚度不足而引起较大的系统动态误差时，也可以采取修正夹具定位元件的方法进行补偿。对一些切削力较大，振动也大的夹具，还应尽可能降低夹具的重心，工件的加工表面应尽可能靠近工作台，以提高夹具的稳定性。

三、非标自动化设备夹具设计的发展趋势

（1）标准化：夹具在实现通用性的前提下，为降低夹具本身的成本，朝着标准化的方向发展，在通用夹具、组合夹具的基础上，制造的夹具应尽量与标准化机床配套，有利于促进机床夹具本身的商品化和规模化生产，降低夹具自身成本。

（2）精密化：随着社会各行业对机械加工产品的精度要求越来越高，现代机床夹具已向着高精密化的方向发展，夹具的精密化主要体现在夹具结构的设计上，在对夹具进行结构设计时要充分发挥主观能动性，以实现机械加工向着更高精度的方向发展。

（3）高效化：因加工行业竞争日益激烈，要求机械加工企业要zui大限度提高工作效率，因此对机床夹具也提出了更高的要求，首先能适应高速加工的要求，并zui大程度降低夹具的辅助时间，提高劳动生产率，保持加工的连续性和安全生产，降低了工人的劳动负荷。

（4）柔性化：通过对夹具的结构进行科学设计，将不可拆卸机构改造成可拆卸机构，使之可以通过自身的组合、调整来满足各种工艺的需求，设计出结构更加合理、精度更高、并且可自动拆卸、更换的柔性化夹具，提高夹具的工作效率，从而为现代加工提供更好的支持，也使非标自动化设备夹具的设计制造得到了众多企业的重视。

This webpage is a Chinese industry article from Guangzhou Vefast Automation Equipment Co., Ltd. (广州维发自动化设备有限公司) discussing the design and manufacturing of fixtures (夹具) for non-standard automation equipment, published on March 4, 2023, with 4,667 views.

The article covers three main areas:

1. **Fixture Structure and Clamping Force Design**: Key design points include ensuring the workpiece occupies the correct position after positioning, maintaining position stability and minimizing vibration during processing while avoiding excessive clamping deformation, matching clamping device complexity to production batch size (larger batches permit more complex, higher-efficiency designs), and ensuring good manufacturability and usability with simple structures that use standard fixture components.

2. **Overall Stiffness Design**: The overall rigidity of the fixture has a special impact on dynamic machining errors. When fixture stiffness greatly exceeds other components, dynamic errors depend mainly on manufacturing and installation precision. For fixtures with high cutting forces and vibrations, the center of gravity should be lowered and work surfaces placed close to the worktable for stability. Fixture positioning elements can also be corrected to compensate for system dynamic errors.

3. **Development Trends**: Four key trends are identified:
   - **Standardization**: Reducing costs through standard fixtures compatible with standardized machine tools to enable commercialization and scale production.
   - **Precision**: Moving toward high-precision fixture designs as product accuracy requirements increase across industries.
   - **High Efficiency**: Adapting to high-speed machining, minimizing auxiliary time, improving productivity, maintaining production continuity and safety while reducing worker labor load.
   - **Flexibility**: Transforming non-detachable structures into detachable ones that can be combined and adjusted to meet various process needs, enabling automatic disassembly and replacement of flexible fixtures.

The company footer describes Guangzhou Vefast Automation Equipment Co., Ltd. as an automation systems integrator focused on R&D, design, manufacturing, assembly, debugging, sales, and service of intelligent factory equipment, specializing in three industries: personal computers & servers, medical/biological, and semiconductor & new materials.

# Raise3D 3D 打印赋能夹具设计：重构工业制造效率新范式

举报

在工业生产的精密装配、检测与加工环节中，夹具作为定位与固定工件的核心工具，直接决定了生产精度与效率。传统夹具设计依赖 CNC 加工等工艺，存在开发周期长、定制成本高、迭代灵活度不足等痛点。Raise3D 凭借全球 50,000 + 企业验证的 3D 打印技术实力，构建起覆盖设备、软件、材料与服务的全流程夹具设计解决方案，为多行业提供高效、精准、柔性的夹具制造新路径。

### 一、工业夹具设计的核心痛点与 3D 打印解决方案

传统夹具设计与制造模式在现代柔性生产体系中逐渐显露短板，而 Raise3D 基于 FFF/FDM、SLS 等技术的 3D 打印方案，针对性破解行业核心难题。

#### 1.1 传统夹具设计的四大核心瓶颈

1. **开发周期漫长**：CNC 加工需经过图纸深化、刀路编程、机床调试等多环节，一套定制夹具平均开发周期长达 1-2 周，难以匹配快速迭代的生产需求。
2. **定制成本高昂**：小批量夹具生产时，机床调试成本占比超 40%，复杂结构需多部件拼接，额外增加材料与装配成本。
3. **结构设计受限**：传统加工难以实现复杂内腔、镂空支撑等优化结构，夹具自重较大且定位精度易受装配误差影响。
4. **迭代灵活性差**：产品更新后需重新设计加工夹具，旧夹具多面临报废，造成材料浪费与时间损耗。

#### 1.2 Raise3D 3D 打印的夹具设计优势

Raise3D 通过技术创新实现夹具设计全链路优化，核心优势体现在以下维度：

| 对比维度 | 传统 CNC 加工模式 | Raise3D 3D 打印模式 | 技术支撑来源 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 开发周期 | 7-14 天 | 1-3 天 | 行业实践验证 |
| 制造成本 | 小批量单价高（调试成本占比 40%+） | 降低 30%-60%（无复杂调试环节） | 企业应用数据 |
| 最小精度 | ±0.1mm | ±0.01mm（极限层厚） | Raise3D Pro2 Plus 参数 |
| 结构自由度 | 受加工方式限制，复杂结构需拼接 | 一体成型复杂内腔、镂空结构 | FFF/SLS 技术特性 |
| 设备占地 | 大型机床（≥2㎡） | 最小仅 620×590mm（可推动移动） | Raise3D Pro2 Plus 尺寸 |

**结论**：3D 打印技术从成本、效率与设计自由度三个维度重构夹具制造逻辑，尤其适配小批量、定制化、快迭代的夹具需求。

### 二、Raise3D 夹具设计核心技术矩阵

Raise3D 以设备为核心、软件为中枢、材料为基础，构建起闭环的夹具设计技术体系，确保每一套 3D 打印夹具都满足工业级应用标准。

#### 2.1 高精度打印设备：夹具成型的核心保障

针对不同夹具尺寸与精度需求，Raise3D 提供全系列设备选择，覆盖从实验室研发到工厂批量生产的全场景。

##### （1）工厂级主力机型：Pro2 Plus

作为工业场景的标杆机型，Pro2 Plus 专为工装夹具生产优化，核心参数与优势如下：

* **成型能力**：305×305×605mm 成型空间，可单次打印多套小型夹具或完整大型定位治具。
* **精度控制**：极限层厚低至 0.01mm，满足定位孔、插销等关键结构的装配需求。
* **环境适配**：支持 7/24 小时连续运行，可适应工厂车间复杂工况环境。
* **空间优势**：占地面积仅 620×590mm，采用可推动设计，可灵活部署于工程师办公区或生产车间。

##### （2）柔性材料专用机型：E3

针对柔性夹具与复合结构需求，E3 通过技术创新突破材料打印瓶颈：

* **柔性材料适配**：搭载 FlexFeed 柔性材料辅助进料套件，TPU 打印速度可达 200mm/s 且质量稳定。
* **多模式打印**：独立双喷头（IDEX）支持双色 / 双材料打印，可实现夹具刚性主体与柔性接触部的一体成型。
* **智能调平**：9 点自动调平系统确保喷嘴与平台距离精准控制，打印成功率提升至 95% 以上。

##### （3）精密批量生产机型：RMS220

面向高精密夹具批量需求，RMS220 采用 SLS 激光烧结技术，具备以下优势：

* **精度表现**：成型精度达 ±0.2mm，支持最小 0.5mm 壁厚（PA11 材料），适配连接器检测夹具等精密场景。
* **生产效率**：每日制件产量最高 5 公斤（PA12 材料），打印速度 2.2L/h（20% 填充密度）。
* **材料兼容**：支持 PA12、PA11、TPU 等多种粉末材料，粉末切换时间仅 45 分钟，为多类型夹具生产提供灵活选择。

#### 2.2 全流程软件系统：夹具设计的数字化中枢

Raise3D 自主研发的软件生态实现夹具设计从建模到打印的全流程管控，大幅降低操作门槛。

##### （1）ideaMaker 切片软件

作为夹具打印的核心控制工具，该软件具备三大核心能力：

1. **路径优化**：针对夹具受力特点智能规划打印路径，相比传统切片软件减少 50% TPU 材料拉丝问题，确保定位面光滑度。
2. **参数预设**：内置 100 + 工程材料参数库，包含夹具常用的 PETG、PA、TPU 等材料的最优打印参数，直接调用即可保障成型质量。
3. **结构预览**：支持打印过程模拟与结构强度预览，提前规避支撑失效、变形等问题。

##### （2）RaiseCloud 云平台

为多设备生产场景提供协同管理能力：

* **任务排程**：集中管理多台打印机任务，自动分配打印资源，设备空置率降低 30% 以上。
* **远程监控**：实时查看夹具打印进度与设备状态，工程师无需现场值守，节省人力成本。
* **数据沉淀**：自动存储打印参数与成品数据，为后续夹具迭代提供数据支撑。

#### 2.3 工程级材料体系：夹具性能的基础支撑

Raise3D 通过开放材料生态与认证体系，确保夹具材料满足不同工况需求：

* **结构类材料**：工业级 PETG ESD、Hyper Speed PLA Pro 等，具备高强度、抗冲击特性，适配定位治具主体结构。
* **柔性材料**：硬度 80A 以上的 TPU/TPE/TPEE 材料，用于夹具接触部，避免工件表面划伤。
* **耐高温材料**：适配金属加工场景的耐高温工程塑料，可承受 150℃以上持续高温。
* **认证体系**：通过 OFP 项目与主流材料品牌合作认证，确保材料与设备匹配性，工艺稳定性提升 40%。

### 三、典型行业夹具设计应用案例与实践效果

Raise3D 夹具设计解决方案已在工业制造、消费电子、科研等多领域落地，通过实际案例验证技术价值。

#### 3.1 工业物联网：研华科技柔性工装精益生产案例

研华科技作为全球知名工业物联网企业，其昆山工厂面临多型号控制器装配的夹具需求，传统 CNC 加工模式难以匹配快速换产需求。

##### 项目痛点

* 每月需开发 8-10 套定制化定位治具，CNC 加工周期长导致产线换产延迟。
* 控制器外壳为薄壁结构，传统金属夹具易造成装配划伤，合格率仅 92%。

##### 解决方案

研华科技引入 Raise3D Pro2 Plus 打印机生产定位治具，采用工业级 PETG 材料一体成型。

##### 实施效果

1. **周期缩短**：单套夹具开发周期从 7 天压缩至 2 天，产线换产响应速度提升 71%。
2. **精度达标**：0.01mm 极限层厚确保定位孔与插销的精准装配，装配误差控制在 ±0.05mm 以内。
3. **成本优化**：小批量生产场景下，单套夹具成本降低 45%，年节省工装费用超 20 万元。
4. **质量提升**：塑料夹具与薄壁工件柔性接触，装配合格率提升至 99.5%。

#### 3.2 精密制造：日本武藏精密耐温夹具案例

日本武藏精密专注于小型精密零部件生产，其检测环节需要定制化耐温夹具，用于高温环境下的尺寸检测。

##### 项目痛点

* 传统金属夹具自重较大，导致检测过程中工件定位偏移，检测误差超 0.1mm。
* 检测环境温度达 120℃，普通塑料夹具易变形失效。

##### 解决方案

采用 Raise3D 打印机搭配耐高温工程塑料，一体成型镂空结构检测夹具。

##### 实施效果

1. **轻量化设计**：镂空结构使夹具自重降低 60%，定位偏移量控制在 0.02mm 以内。
2. **耐温性能**：120℃环境下持续工作无变形，使用寿命达 10,000 次以上。
3. **效率提升**：夹具开发周期从 10 天缩短至 3 天，满足快速迭代的检测需求。

* **材料定制认证**：根据特殊工况需求，协助客户完成新型材料的打印参数调试与认证。

### 五、FAQ：Raise3D 夹具设计解决方案常见问题

1. **问：3D 打印夹具的精度能否满足工业级装配需求？** 答：完全可以。Raise3D Pro2 Plus 机型极限层厚达 0.01mm，RMS220 机型成型精度 ±0.2mm，可满足定位孔、插销等关键结构的装配要求，研华科技等企业已通过实际应用验证其精度达标。
2. **问：3D 打印夹具的使用寿命与传统金属夹具有差距吗？** 答：在非极端磨损场景下，采用工程级材料（如 PA、PETG）的 3D 打印夹具使用寿命可达传统塑料夹具的 2-3 倍，部分增强材料夹具可实现 10,000 次以上循环使用，且更换成本更低。
3. **问：小批量夹具生产选择哪种机型更合适？** 答：单套或小批量（≤5 套）夹具建议选择 Pro2 Plus，305×305×605mm 成型空间可满足多数中小型夹具需求；若涉及柔性材料或双色结构，E3 机型的 FlexFeed 套件与双喷头设计更具优势；批量生产（≥10 套 / 批次）则推荐 RMS220，日均产量可达 5 公斤，效率更高。
4. **问：没有 3D 建模基础能否使用 Raise3D 的夹具设计方案？** 答：可以。Raise3D 提供标准化夹具模型库，支持参数化修改（如定位孔位置、夹持尺寸），配合 ideaMaker 软件的预设参数，零基础用户经过 1 天培训即可独立完成简单夹具的打印生产。
5. **问：3D 打印夹具的后处理复杂吗？需要额外设备吗？** 答：多数夹具打印后仅需简单处理：支撑去除可通过手动或专用工具完成，表面精度要求较高的定位面可通过砂纸打磨优化，无需额外大型后处理设备。RMS220 机型打印的 SLS 部件甚至可直接使用，无需支撑去除环节。

**1. Core Pain Points & 3D Printing Solution:**
Traditional CNC-based fixture manufacturing faces four key bottlenecks: long development cycles (1-2 weeks), high customization costs (machine setup exceeds 40% of costs for small batches), structural design limitations (complex internal cavities require assembly), and poor iteration flexibility. Raise3D's 3D printing addresses these with: development cycles reduced from 7-14 days to 1-3 days, cost reduction of 30-60%, minimum precision of ±0.01mm (vs ±0.1mm for CNC), and one-piece forming of complex structures.

**2. Raise3D Core Technology Matrix:**
- **Pro2 Plus (factory-grade)**: 305×305×605mm build volume, ultra-thin layer depth down to 0.01mm, 7/24 continuous operation, footprint of only 620×590mm with movable design.
- **E3 (flexible materials)**: Features FlexFeed kit supporting TPU printing at 200mm/s, independent dual-nozzle (IDEX) for dual-color/dual-material printing, 9-point auto leveling with 95%+ print success rate.
- **RMS220 (precision batch production)**: SLS laser sintering, ±0.2mm accuracy, minimum 0.5mm wall thickness (PA11), daily output up to 5kg (PA12), print speed 2.2L/h, supports PA12/PA11/TPU powders with 45-minute powder changeover.
- **ideaMaker software**: Smart path optimization (reduces TPU stringing by 50%), 100+ built-in engineering material parameter presets, print simulation and structural strength preview.
- **RaiseCloud platform**: Multi-device task scheduling (reduces idle rate by 30%+), remote monitoring, data storage for iteration.
- **Materials**: PETG ESD, Hyper Speed PLA Pro, TPU/TPE/TPEE (80A+ hardness), high-temperature plastics (150°C+), OFP certification program improving process stability by 40%.

**3. Case Studies:**
- **Advantech (研华科技, industrial IoT)**: Kunsan factory needed 8-10 custom fixtures monthly. Using Pro2 Plus with PETG: development cycle cut from 7 to 2 days (71% faster line changeover), assembly error within ±0.05mm, 45% cost reduction (saving 200,000+ RMB annually), and qualified rate improved from 92% to 99.5%.
- **Musashi Seimitsu (Japan, precision manufacturing)**: Needed high-temperature detection fixtures. Using high-temp engineering plastic with hollow structure: 60% weight reduction (positioning deviation within 0.02mm), sustained operation at 120°C without deformation, 10,000+ cycle lifespan, development time reduced from 10 to 3 days.

**4. Full-Service Process:** Five-step standard service (needs diagnosis, design, free sample production, batch deployment, 7×24 support) plus value-added services (MES system development, material certification, training).

**5. FAQ highlights:** 3D printed fixtures meet industrial assembly precision requirements; lifespan is 2-3× traditional plastic fixtures (up to 10,000+ cycles); Pro2 Plus suits small batches (≤5 sets), E3 for flexible/dual-color needs, RMS220 for volume production (≥10 sets/batch); no 3D modeling background needed (1-day training); post-processing is simple with most parts usable directly.

This is a product information page from Siemens about NX for Manufacturing, specifically focusing on Tooling and Fixture Design capabilities within the NX software platform. The page is presented in Simplified Chinese (auto-translated) and covers the following key areas:

**Tooling and Fixture Design Capabilities:**
1. **Mold Design** - Uses advanced tools to verify part design, mold design, and motion to accelerate mold development. Uses standard parts, component systems, and mold base libraries to configure mold structures. Features advanced functions, step-by-step guidance, and associativity with part models for quick response to design changes and high-quality molds.
2. **Progressive Die Design** - Automates the most tedious tasks and simplifies complex progressive die design processes. Provides comprehensive solutions for both straight-cut and free-form sheet metal parts, maintaining associativity with part design at every stage.
3. **Stamping Die Design** - Advanced features for automotive stamping dies, including formability analysis, die planning, die face design, detailed die structure design, and die verification. Guides definition of manufacturing processes for complex stamped parts, representing the stamping line and sheet metal shapes at each press.
4. **Electrode Design** - Automates the entire EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining) process from design to production. Efficiently models the most complex and challenging electrodes. Electrode design is associative, ensuring design changes to cores and cavities propagate seamlessly to electrodes and into machining.
5. **Fixture Design** - Uses latest dynamic modeling and assembly tools to accelerate design of jigs and fixtures fully associative with 3D part models. Includes interactive assembly features for positioning fixture components, automatic drawing/document creation, kinematic simulation (e.g., open/close positions), and strength/deformation checks.

**Case Study:**
- Cavalier Tool and Manufacturing, an award-winning mold maker located in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, uses Siemens Designcenter software.

- NX X Manufacturing CAD/CAM Standard: 2.5-axis milling, hole making, turning, and on-machine probing with cloud technology
- NX X Manufacturing CAD/CAM Advanced: 3-axis milling for free-form parts (cloud-based)

The article addresses the management challenges of multi-variety, small-batch (MVSB) manufacturing, which is increasingly common in modern manufacturing due to market demands for product diversity.

The article outlines 8 key strategies for managing MVSB production:

1. **Optimizing Production Planning and Scheduling**: Use advanced production management systems (specifically recommending 简道云's production management system with BOM management, production planning, scheduling, work reporting, and production monitoring capabilities), apply data analysis tools (Excel or ERP) for demand forecasting, implement flexible rolling plans, and adopt lean production principles.

3. **Enhancing Production Flexibility**: Introduce flexible production systems with automated equipment, implement modular production by decomposing processes into modules, promote standardized operations, and strengthen employee training for multi-skilled workers.

6. **Effective Cost Control**: Conduct cost analysis of production, material, and labor costs, promote lean production to reduce waste, strengthen cost management systems, and introduce ERP-based cost control tools.

7. **Improving Team Collaboration and Execution**: Strengthen team building through activities, implement goal management (MBO), enhance communication through regular team meetings, and improve employee incentive systems with performance assessment.

8. **Managing Production Plans, Inventory, and Efficiency in Practice**: The article's FAQ section addresses three specific challenges including meeting order deadlines, reducing inventory pressure/overstock, and improving production efficiency amidst complex workflows.

The article strongly recommends 简道云's production management system as the primary solution, with a trial link to www.jiandaoyun.com.
